quotedTweet.rawContent:
Cool idea, but I think this highlights how difficult it is to reduce OPSEC to an AI score.

A lot of OPSEC checks are deterministic. You don't need an LLM to tell you that running default BloodHound collection, dropping mimikatz.exe, or using a known command line is noisy.

The hard part is actual evasion, because that is holistic and environment-specific:

- EDR configuration
- SIEM ingestion
- SOC/MSSP capability
- custom detections
- identity providers
- logging coverage

what is considered normal in that environment

PsExec might be completely normal in one network and immediately suspicious in another.

An AI model usually does not have enough of that context. By the time it learns what is actually detectable, you may have already generated the telemetry you're trying to avoid.

So IMO Jev is useful as a classifier / warning system, but an 'OPSEC score' should not be confused with real-world evasion.

Building an evasion harness is significantly harder than building a pentest harness.

Wouldn't you agree?

I feel like you are proofing my point lol.

➡️ > "I built a pretty successful company that focused on prioritizing attackable surface area on that exact premise."

So you admit that not everybody can do it themselves? I wonder what experience you have, and they don't? Is it maybe experience about how systems could get exploited? :P

Whether people get distracted by exploitability or not seems to be a question about effective communication, and not about whether this is important data. I am saying you have the experience (from the history of vulnerabilities), to judge whether a system has a particular risk or not. And without that experience, you couldn't implement meaningful mitigations.

➡️ > "Meanwhile, you don't need to know a device has a history of exploitability or active exploits to know if the admin interface on your VPN should be publicly accessible on the internet. The VPN crosses a security boundary and admins has elevated privileges."

I think you don't realise how much experience (from vulnerabilities) you put into that sentence. I know it seems trivial and obvious to you, but it is not obvious without your knowledge. 

The VPN port requires authentication, and the admin interface requires authentication. There are only two reason why you know it's safer to expose the VPN port to the internet, but not safe to expose the admin interface:
1. you have seen almost no critical vulnerabilities in eg. OpenVPN, despite a lot of people looking
2. or, you have seen exactly this VPN product, or similar products, getting vulnerabilities on the admin interface

> I don't need to know anything about image parsing at all and I can tell you having my internal chat server connected to the public internet needs an extraordinary amount of attention, visibility, logging and alerting. If that service starts enumerating the metadata server, spawning unexpected process or crashing for any reason I want to know as soon as possible as something bad is probably happening.

Yeah sure. But monitoring is very resource intensive, it's reactive and not catching all attacks. An image exploit doesn't have to crash anything, the payload can re-use the existing database connection, read data from the heap and send it out the data as a legit HTTP response. So yes, you still have to know that this is a risky component that needs extra isolation.

➡️ > "If there was a direct path from a CSS parser to something critical to my business surviving then I would consider sandboxing or otherwise limiting what CSS could get into that CSS parser."

I don't think you actually mean that. Because CSS parsing (as far as I know) hasn't been a common place for vulnerabilities. However maybe you come to this conclusion because "parsers" tend to be risky and we know increased complexity leads to increased exploitability. So with this experience it makes sense to be suspicious of parsers.

But then why are you are not putting all the JSON parsers into a sandbox???? Why is not every API endpoint getting the special treatment?

To me the answer is obvious: we have experience from seeing what does and doesn't get exploited. This tells us what needs to be sandboxed and what doesn't.

➡️ > "I also think so much focus on exploits can sometimes hurt our understanding of that."

I guess you are saying that, because companies turned developers into Jira-ticket-robots. I am also advocating for mitigations that can get rid of entire bug-classes, and build secure architectures that stop exploitation chains, or add another layer in the swiss-cheese model. 

Also I find it ridiculous to say we should not focus on exploits. Exploits are the root of anything hacking (let's ignore social engineering etc.). Without exploits there wouldn't be any need for this conversation at all. Defense-in-depth is supposed to protect you against exploits. So without the data from all these exploits we wouldn't know how to defend against them.

My point is that the data from vulnerabilities is useful and we should use that data to build mitigations. And not sell snakeoil security products that protect you from something made up. Also I am convinced you act (maybe subconsciously?) upon exploitation experience, whether you acknowledge this or not. You are doing exactly what I am saying: you turn exploitation experience into effective mitigations.

Also we are in a new era with AI. And maybe we could try something crazy?! Just putting this out there as another hypothesis:

How often do we see critical remote vulnerabilities in OpenSSH? This shows that it does seem possible to build secure software by fixing vulnerabilities (and there are many examples like nginx, OpenVPN, ...). The problem has always been software written faster than we can secure it. Maybe AI makes it worse, or maybe it makes it better! Maybe we can just let go 100.000 agents and we get any software to the level of OpenSSH? If AI gets cheap enough, that could be realistic.

But where do we apply AI effectively today? I don't think AI scales the education of developers to build secure architectures. Or having companies doing consulting one-by-one. But it seems like OpenAI could deploy an army of agents, get rid of a massive amount of bugs (in depenencies). And I think that would help A LOT. And even if it would not help directly, the data from that exercise would be extremely valuable. You wouldn't just learn which software is more vulnerable, you would see patterns about which programming languages or coding patterns are problematic, what kind of software is risky, which mitigations hold up, etc. And with that you can can very easily get your customers to rebuild architecture accordingly.

RT @Marmstrongwow: I'm seeing a lot of discourse about who WoW Forever is being made for and while I cannot speak for anyone else on the team I can speak for myself. I am making WoW forever for the classic gamer and for the millions of people who have had their accounts lapse over the years because they were not satisfied with changes that were made to the game. Whether those changes were to the art style, the story, social aspects, game design, or changes to their favorite class. 

I did not spend the last year of my life relearning and mastering how to do things like we did it 20+ years ago for retail players. I could have taken it easy and just kept doing things like I had done for the past 8 years on retail...because I was much more familiar with it and it actually takes a lot less time to do (height maps on textures do a ton of heavy lifting). Because the reality is that the majority of retail players wouldn't care and would probably actually prefer it. But I felt I had a duty to uphold an artistic vision and integrity that millions of people expect from us. But not just for our players, but for my co-workers past and present who worked on it over 20 years ago. If I could not create something that resembled their work then I failed not only them...but myself.

Please do not take this as me throwing any shade at retail players or the retail team because I am one myself...but I wanted to make Forever as authentic of a Vanilla experience as possible. This involves making decisions wildly different than retail. It means holding the line against changes that create a domino affect down the road. It means keeping friction and inconveniences in the game. It means finding friends and forming groups with strangers and being social!! Because WoWs social aspects have always been the pillar of the game and over the years it has slowly been chiseled away at with changes that allow you play alone.

Since the day I started working on the Riverglades I have lived by three sayings.

"Convenience is the death of the journey."

"If you're making a game for everyone then you're making it for no one."

"Every change we make incurs a debt to the authenticity of the game and sooner or later that debt will be paid."

These are my core beliefs and I had a specific group of people I was targeting with my work. These beliefs cannot be shaken and I will try to hold the line against anything that goes against them and will continue to pester the team about things that feel out of place.

That being said, my hope is that Forever will pull in as many people as possible, whether you are a retail gamer, a classic gamer, someone who hasn't played in years, or even a new player. I hope you can all remember what made this game so special in the first place and that starts with understanding why we are so passionate about keeping it authentic.

You don't have to worry about lateral movement or recon stuffs, because most of the high-quality custom BOFs are already ported by default on Vanguard.

our goal is simple. build a high quality framework that remains affordable and actually delivers what operators actually need.

quotedTweet.rawContent:
Frontier models have lowered the bar for discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. This has resulted in an increase of CVEs and workload for both SWE and vulnerability management teams.

And yet the norms around coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines have remained around 90 days. This timeline worked 10 years ago, but is unlikely to survive much longer. We need to move closer to a window of 30 days.

But in order to do this we need to rely on those same models to accurately fix those vulnerabilities and coordinate the release and deployment of new versions. The primary blocker here seems to be confidence in those models to do that job well, and reluctance to remove humans from that loop.

Every day the probability of another shellshock, log4j, or heartbleed rises. If you were in the trenches for those events then you know how difficult it was to track vulnerable assets, test and deploy patches, and ensure the risk was mitigated.

We shouldn’t wait for a crisis like this to rethink and change these norms. We need to move much faster and that requires shorter disclosure timelines, and removing humans from the vulnerability management loop.
